learningPath.title: Connected Learning
learningPath.description: The connected learning path. Competencies demonstrated in one course are reused by later courses rather than duplicated.

course.title: Networking Foundations
course.description: Start from nothing and build a working mental model of how two machines reach each other. You will meet the devices a network is made of, watch traffic move inside one network, learn the two identities a machine carries, work out the decision every machine makes about where to send something, follow a message across a boundary and back, test whether it truly arrived, and repair a simple failure. Before this course you need only the ability to operate a computer, use a keyboard and mouse, navigate a web application, and compare two numbers. No networking vocabulary is assumed: every term you need is introduced here, after you have already seen the behaviour it names.

modules.title: One Network
modules.description: What a network is made of, and how something gets from one machine to another when both are on the same network. Everything here happens inside a single network; boundaries come later.

modules.title: Addresses and Boundaries
modules.description: The second identity a machine carries, and the decision it makes with it: is what I am trying to reach on my own network, or somewhere else? This is the question the rest of the course depends on.

modules.title: Reaching Another Network
modules.description: What a machine does when the answer is "somewhere else": who it hands the message to, what that device does with it, and what the whole trip looks like from one end to the other.

modules.title: Prove It and Fix It
modules.description: Establishing whether something genuinely works rather than appears to, and what to do when it does not. The failure here is bounded and visible; finding a fault you were not shown belongs to a later course.

missions.title: Mission 1 — Follow something across a network
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: operate a computer, and compare two numbers. Nothing else.

When you print a document on a network printer, your computer has to get the print request from where you are sitting to the printer itself. In this mission you follow that request across a small network and see which devices it passes through.

First you meet the devices a small network is made of: the machines people use, the device in the middle that connects them, and the device at the edge that connects this network to other networks. You see where each one sits and what it is attached to.

Then you follow one print request from the computer that sent it to the printer that produces it, predicting where it goes before you watch it happen.

This mission does not teach how the device in the middle makes its decision, and it does not teach what the device at the edge does. Both are deliberate. You will finish with two specific questions, and the missions that follow answer them.

Nothing is configured or changed here. You are learning to read a network before you are asked to alter one.

content.title: Follow something across a network
paragraphs: When you print a document on a network printer, your computer has to get the print request from where you are sitting to the printer itself. The request does not arrive there by magic. It travels, and it passes through other devices on the way.
In this mission you follow one print request across a small network and see which devices it passes through.

You will learn what a network is at a basic level, what a host is, what a network connection represents, where a switch sits in a small network, and how to follow information from one device to another.
You will configure nothing and change nothing. You are learning to read a network before you are asked to alter one.

content.title: What is a host?
paragraphs: Computers on a network are often called hosts. A desktop, a laptop or a server connected to a network can be a host, and so is the phone in your pocket.
A host is where information starts, or where it finishes. PC-A and PC-B are hosts in the network you are about to see.

A printer connected to the network is a host too. The diagrams in this course label a printer as a printer so that you can recognise it at a glance, but for the purpose of getting information from one place to another, it behaves exactly as a computer does.

content.title: Network connections
paragraphs: Devices communicate through network connections. A host does not join a network by being near it: every host has a specific place where the connection arrives — the socket at the back of a laptop, the aerial inside a phone. That connection point is called an interface.
A device built to hold many connections usually calls each one a port rather than an interface. Port and interface name the same idea, and this course uses whichever word the device itself would use.
The connection running between two interfaces is called a link. PC-A has one link, so everything PC-A puts onto this network leaves the same way, and that link is its way in.

content.title: The device in the middle, and the device at the edge
paragraphs: Not every device on a network is a host. A small network also contains devices whose only job is to carry traffic between the hosts, and you can tell them apart by what each one is attached to.

One device sits in the middle. Every host has one link, and every one of those links ends at this same device, each host on a port of its own. No host has a link to another host, so anything travelling between two hosts passes through the device in the middle. That device is called a switch, and this one is named Switch-1.

One device sits at the edge. It is attached to Switch-1, and it is also attached to a connection that leads out of this network entirely. That second attachment is what makes it a different kind of device. It is called a router, and this one is named Router-1.

We will not use Router-1 in this mission. It is here so that you can recognise a router and see where one sits, because Router-1 marks the point where this local network stops. You will discover why it is there in a later mission.

content.caption: Follow the print request. Someone at PC-A wants to print a document using the network printer, so PC-A sends a print request. Follow it from PC-A to the Printer. Select any device to read what it is and what it connects to.
content.textEquivalent: A small network of five devices. Three of them are hosts: PC-A and PC-B are computers people use, and the Printer is the network printer. Each host has one network interface and one link, and every one of those links runs to Switch-1 — PC-A to port 1, PC-B to port 2, the Printer to port 3. Switch-1 is the device in the middle: Switch-1 holds four ports, and every local connection in this network arrives at one of them. Router-1 is attached to Switch-1 on port 4 through its local port, and Router-1 also has a second, outward port whose connection leads away from this network entirely. No link joins two hosts directly, so any path between two hosts runs through Switch-1. Someone at PC-A wants to print a document, so PC-A sends a print request towards the Printer. You are asked to predict which device the print request reaches first. The print request leaves PC-A along PC-A's single link and arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 then passes it on, and the print request arrives at the Printer over the link that ends on Switch-1 port 3, where the Printer accepts the print job. The walkthrough is then complete. PC-B and Router-1 receive nothing and are not visited. How Switch-1 works out which port leads to the Printer is Mission 2, and what Router-1 does is Mission 5 and Mission 6. You can select any device at any point to read what it is, which interfaces it has, and what it connects to.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the computer a person is working at, and it is where this print request begins. It has one network connection, and that connection runs to Switch-1.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is a second computer on this local network, connected to Switch-1 the same way PC-A is. It is here because a network is shared: several machines connect to the same switch, each on a connection of its own. This print request came from PC-A, so PC-B plays no part in it.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is the shared network printer, and it is what this print request is for. It is a host like PC-A and PC-B, with a connection into Switch-1 of its own, which is what lets any computer on this network send it work.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 is the device in the middle of this local network. PC-A, PC-B, the Printer and Router-1 each connect to a port on it, so anything one of them sends arrives at Switch-1 first. Mission 2 explains how Switch-1 decides which port to send it out of.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 sits at the edge of this local network, with one port facing Switch-1 and one port leading away. It is the way out when a machine here needs to reach something that is not on this network. This print request does not use Router-1, because PC-A and the Printer are both on this local network. Mission 5 explains why a computer sends traffic to a router when what it wants is somewhere else.

stages.narration: The print request leaves PC-A along PC-A's single link.
stages.decision: PC-A is the computer sending the print request. It has one link, so everything PC-A sends leaves the same way.

prediction.prompt: PC-A sends the print request towards the Printer. Which device does the print request reach first?
options: The Printer
Switch-1
Router-1

stages.narration: The print request arrives at Switch-1, on port 1.
stages.decision: PC-A's link ends at port 1 on Switch-1, so Switch-1 is the first device the print request reaches. But the print request is meant for the Printer, so what does Switch-1 do with it? That is what Mission 2 begins investigating; continue to see where the print request goes.

stages.narration: The print request arrives at the Printer, and the Printer accepts the print job.
stages.decision: The Printer connects to Switch-1 on port 3, and that link carried the print request the rest of the way. The document a user asked for at PC-A has reached the machine that will produce it.

confirmation.narration: The print request reached the network printer, and the printer accepted the print job.
confirmation.summary: PC-A sent it, Switch-1 was in the middle, and the Printer received it. You have followed one print request from the machine that sent it to the machine it was for. Now you may be wondering how Switch-1 knew where to send it, and why the print request did not go through Router-1. Those are the right questions to be left with: Mission 2 answers the first, and Missions 5 and 6 answer the second.

content.title: Reading the picture
paragraphs: The drawing you just worked through has a name. A picture of what is connected to what is called a topology.

A topology is not a floor plan. Two devices drawn beside each other may sit in different rooms, and a line drawn between them may be a cable running through three walls. A topology shows relationships, not distances, and reading a topology as a map of the building is the most common way to misread one.

You can now do something that every mission after this one depends on: look at a small network, say what each device is for, name the link between any two devices, and say which device a message must pass through to get from one host to another.

missions.title: Mission 2 — Inside one network: how a switch delivers
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a small network and name its devices and connections (Mission 1).

Two machines are connected to the same device in the middle. Someone at one of them sends a file to a colleague at the other. Watch what happens the first time, and then watch what happens the second time. They are not the same, and the difference is the whole of this mission.

The first time, the device in the middle does not know where the destination is, so it sends a copy of the file out of every other connection at once and lets the right machine answer. That is wasteful, and it does not stay that way. The device pays attention to which connection each delivery arrives on, records what it observes, and the next one goes to exactly one place.

Once you have seen that happen, you get the words for it. Each machine carries a built-in identity set at the factory, written in a notation you will recognise but do not need to calculate with. The unit of traffic that carries one of these identities to another has a name. The record the middle device builds up has a name. Sending a copy to everyone because you do not yet know better has a name too.

You will also meet the first thing that looks like a failure and is not. Traffic reaching every machine instead of one looks wrong the first time you see it. It is correct, it is temporary, and telling the difference between "broken" and "working as designed" is a habit worth forming early.

By the end you will be able to explain how one machine reaches another inside a single network, why the second attempt behaves differently from the first, and what happens when the destination is not known.

content.title: One file, two machines
paragraphs: Someone at PC-A is sharing a file with a colleague at PC-B. PC-A and PC-B are on the same small network, each with a link into Switch-1, and no other device stands between them.
PC-A addresses the file to PC-B's interface. PC-A can do that because it already holds an identity for that interface — a value naming which connection point on the network the file is for.

How PC-A came to hold that identity is a real question with a real answer, and the answer needs one idea you do not have yet. The question is not being waved away: Mission 4 answers it. For now, take it as given that PC-A knows which interface it is addressing, and watch what the network does with the file.
You will watch this twice. The same file is sent to the same machine on two separate occasions, and the two occasions do not go the same way. The difference between them is the whole of this mission.

content.caption: An instructional walkthrough of two deliveries on one network. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A small network of four devices: three hosts — PC-A, PC-B and a Printer — each with one interface, and Switch-1 in the middle holding three ports. PC-A is on port 1, PC-B on port 2, the Printer on port 3. Each host interface carries a hardware identity, which you can read in the inspector. Someone at PC-A is sending a file to a colleague at PC-B, and the walkthrough follows that file being sent twice. The first time, PC-A puts the file onto its connection addressed to PC-B, and it arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 holds no record of where PC-B is, so at that same moment it sends a copy of the file out of both of its other connections at once — port 2 and port 3. These are two copies of one delivery, not two separate files. The copy on port 2 reaches PC-B, which is the machine the file is addressed to, and PC-B accepts it. The copy on port 3 reaches the Printer, which compares the file's destination against its own identity, sees that they are different, and does not accept it; nothing has gone wrong there. As the file arrived, Switch-1 recorded what it could see: the file came in on port 1 from PC-A, so PC-A is on port 1. Switch-1 still has no record of PC-B. PC-B then replies, and that reply arrives at Switch-1 on port 2, which is how Switch-1 records that PC-B is on port 2. The reply leaves by port 1 alone and reaches PC-A, because Switch-1 already knew where PC-A was. The second time, PC-A sends the same file to PC-B again and nothing about the file has changed. Switch-1 receives it on port 1, finds PC-B already recorded against port 2, and sends it out of port 2 only. Port 3 stays quiet and the Printer sees nothing at all. The file reaches PC-B. What changed between the two deliveries is not the file: it is what Switch-1 had recorded from the ordinary traffic it saw in between.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the computer sending the file, in both of the deliveries this walkthrough follows. It connects to port 1 on Switch-1, and it addresses the file to PC-B's interface.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is the machine the file is meant for, both times it is sent. It connects to port 2 on Switch-1, and its interface carries the hardware identity PC-A addresses the file to.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is a third host on this network, connected to port 3. The file is not meant for it either time. Watch what reaches the Printer during the first delivery and what does not reach it during the second, because the difference between those two moments is the whole of this mission.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 connects all three hosts, one to each port. Everything in this walkthrough arrives here first, and what Switch-1 does with it changes between the first delivery and the second. What it records in between is the subject of this mission.

stages.narration: The person at PC-A shares a file with a colleague at PC-B. PC-A puts the file onto its connection, addressed to PC-B.
stages.decision: PC-A does not decide how the file will travel. PC-A addresses it and sends it; working out which connection leads where is not PC-A's job.

stages.narration: The file arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 holds no record of where PC-B is, so at that same moment it sends a copy of the file out of both of its other connections at once — port 2 and port 3. These are two copies of one delivery, not two separate files.
stages.decision: Switch-1 is not guessing and it is not giving up. It has one delivery for PC-B and no record of which connection leads there, so it uses every connection it has left. Whichever one PC-B is on, the file arrives.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has only just been switched on. Nothing addressed to PC-B has ever passed through it. What does Switch-1 do with this file?
options: Sends it out of port 2 only, because that is where PC-B is
Sends a copy out of every other connection, because it does not yet know which one leads to PC-B
Holds on to it and asks PC-B where it is

stages.narration: The copy on port 2 reaches PC-B, which is the machine the file is addressed to, so PC-B accepts it. The copy on port 3 reaches the Printer at the same moment. The Printer compares the file's destination against its own identity, sees that they are different, and does not accept it.
stages.decision: Nothing has gone wrong at the Printer. Every machine checks whether an arriving delivery is addressed to it, and leaves it alone when it is not. Meanwhile Switch-1 recorded what it could see as the file came past: the file arrived on port 1 and PC-A sent it, so PC-A is on port 1. Nobody configured that. Switch-1 still has no record of PC-B, because PC-B has not sent anything yet.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has now seen the file arrive from PC-A on port 1. What does Switch-1 know at this point?
options: That PC-A is on port 1
That PC-B is on port 2
Both where PC-A is and where PC-B is
Neither, until someone configures it

facts.label: Copy arrived
facts.value: Not accepted — the file is addressed to PC-B

stages.narration: PC-B answers, and its reply arrives at Switch-1 on port 2.
stages.decision: Switch-1 records this arrival exactly as it recorded the first one: the reply came in on port 2 and PC-B sent it, so PC-B is on port 2. That is the one thing Switch-1 was missing a moment ago, and ordinary traffic supplied it.

stages.narration: The reply leaves by port 1 alone and arrives at PC-A. The Printer's connection stays quiet this time.
stages.decision: Switch-1 already knew that PC-A was on port 1, because it recorded that when the file first came past. The reply therefore never needed to go anywhere else.

stages.narration: A little later, the person at PC-A sends the same file to PC-B again. Nothing about the file itself has changed.
stages.decision: Same sender, same destination, same network, same file. The only thing that is different is what has happened in between.

stages.narration: The file arrives at Switch-1 on port 1 again. This time Switch-1 finds PC-B already recorded against port 2, and sends the file out of port 2 alone. Port 3 stays quiet, and the Printer sees nothing at all.
stages.decision: This is the whole difference. Switch-1 is no cleverer than it was a minute ago. It simply knows one thing now that it did not know then, and it learned that thing by watching ordinary traffic that nobody sent for the purpose.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has now seen a reply arrive from PC-B on port 2. What does it do with this second copy of the file?
options: Sends a copy out of every other connection again
Sends it out of port 2 only
Waits for PC-B to answer before sending anything

stages.narration: The file arrives at PC-B. One copy, one connection, and nothing anywhere else on the network.
stages.decision: Compare that with the first delivery: the same two machines and the same file, but one connection used instead of three.

confirmation.narration: The file reached PC-B directly the second time, and the Printer never saw it.
confirmation.summary: The first time, Switch-1 had no record of where PC-B was, so it sent a copy of the file out of every other connection at once and the file still arrived. Switch-1 recorded where each machine was by watching ordinary traffic arrive — PC-A when the file came past, PC-B when the reply came back. By the second time Switch-1 knew, so one copy out of one connection was enough.

content.title: What you just watched
paragraphs: The first time, Switch-1 had never seen anything addressed to PC-B, so Switch-1 did not know which of its ports led there. Switch-1 did the one thing that reliably works: at the same moment, it sent a copy out of every other connection, so that whichever one led to PC-B, the file would arrive. Sending a copy out of the other connections because the destination has not been learned yet is called flooding.

Flooding is not a failure and not a mistake. Flooding is what a switch does when it does not yet know where a destination is, and it succeeds — the file reached PC-B. Flooding is merely wasteful, because the Printer was handed a copy it had no use for.

Flooding also does not last. Everything arriving at a switch shows which port it came in on and which interface sent it, and a switch keeps a record of what it sees. Switch-1 recorded PC-A against port 1 the instant the file first came past, and PC-B against port 2 the instant PC-B's reply arrived. Switch-1 builds that record out of ordinary traffic, and nobody configures it.

Notice the order. Switch-1 learned where the SENDER was from the very first delivery, because the sender is the one thing an arriving delivery always shows. It could not learn where PC-B was until PC-B sent something of its own — which is why the record had one entry after the first delivery and two after the reply.

By the second delivery Switch-1 had PC-B on that record, so there was nothing to work out: one connection, one copy, and the Printer's connection left quiet. Nothing about the file changed between the two deliveries. What changed is what Switch-1 knew.

content.title: The identity on an interface
paragraphs: The value you could read on each interface in the inspector is the identity PC-A addressed the file to, and the same value is what Switch-1 recorded against a port. That value is called a MAC address.

A MAC address belongs to an interface rather than to a machine, so a laptop with both a socket and an aerial carries two MAC addresses. A MAC address is set when the hardware is made rather than chosen afterwards, and for delivery within one local network it is the identity that matters.

You read a MAC address. You do not calculate with it. A MAC address is written as six pairs of characters separated by colons, and for now that is the whole of what you need to know about the notation.

The record you watched Switch-1 build has a name as well: it is the MAC address table. The walkthrough showed it with device names — PC-A, PC-B — so that you could read it at a glance before you had met the term. What a switch actually stores against each port is the MAC address of the interface it last saw sending there. Same record, same behaviour, written the way the switch holds it.

content.caption: The MAC address of one interface, as a real machine reports it. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Real output carries several more lines and several more fields; this shows only the line that matters here, so that nothing appears which you have not met yet.

content.title: The unit that moved
paragraphs: Something specific travelled from PC-A's interface to a port on Switch-1, and then from a port on Switch-1 to PC-B's interface. That thing carried the address of the interface it was for, and the address of the interface that sent it.
That unit is called a frame. A frame is what moves across one local network, from interface to interface, addressed by the kind of address you have just met.

A second unit exists, with a different name and a different job, and it becomes important the moment something has to leave this network. Naming that second unit now would mean nothing to you, because you have not yet watched anything leave. You meet it in Mission 6, where the difference between the two finally has something to be a difference about.

content.title: Looks wrong, works as designed
paragraphs: The Printer was handed a copy of a file that had nothing to do with the Printer, compared the address on that copy against its own, saw that the two did not match, and did not accept it. Nothing went wrong.

The first time you see traffic arriving somewhere it was not meant for, it looks like a fault. Form the habit now of asking a different question first: is this broken, or is this the system working as designed?
You will need that question for the rest of this course. You will need it most in Mission 8, where something genuinely is broken and telling the difference is the entire job.

missions.title: Mission 3 — IPv4 addresses: the second identity
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: explain how one machine reaches another inside a single network, and what the built-in factory identity is for (Mission 2).

Every machine you have looked at already has an identity. So why does it need a second one?

The factory identity has a problem: it says nothing about where the machine is. It cannot be changed, it follows the hardware, and it is useless for organising anything. A second identity fixes that. It is assigned rather than built in, it is written as four numbers separated by dots, and unlike the first one it can be chosen to say something about which group a machine belongs to.

You will look at real output from a machine and find its second identity, sitting next to the name of the connection that holds it. Reading that output is a small skill with a large payoff: it is how you confirm what a machine actually has, rather than what someone told you it has.

This mission does not yet tell you how a machine uses the second identity to decide anything. That decision needs one more piece of information, and it is the whole of the next mission. Here you are establishing the fact that the identity exists, that it is assigned, that it can be read, and that it is a different kind of thing from the one you met in Mission 2.

Addresses can be set by hand or handed out automatically by another machine. This course sets them by hand so you can see exactly what is where. Machines can also be reached by name rather than by address; that is a separate system, and this course works in addresses deliberately.

By the end you will be able to read a machine's assigned address from real output, say which connection holds it, and explain how it differs from the identity you met in Mission 2. You will use that in every mission that follows, and in every later course that asks you to check what a machine actually has.

content.title: One connection, two identities
paragraphs: In Mission 2 you read an identity off PC-A's connection: a value set when the hardware was made, which Switch-1 recorded against a port so that it knew where PC-A was. That identity did a real job, and it did it well.

Here is the thing that should bother you. That identity says nothing about where PC-A is. It was fixed in a factory before anyone knew which network the machine would be plugged into, it stays the same if you carry the machine to another building, and no part of it can be chosen to mean anything.

Inside one network that did not matter. Switch-1 never needed to know where PC-A was in any larger sense. It only needed to know which of its own ports PC-A was on, and it learned that by watching ordinary traffic arrive.
So the connection already has an identity. Why would it need a second one? Do not take the answer from this page. Look at what a machine actually reports about itself, and find it.

content.caption: PC-A, reporting on the connection you already know by name. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Real output carries several more lines and several more fields than this; two lines are shown, and you met one of them in Mission 2. Before you read on: find the line you have not seen before, and say which connection is holding it.

content.title: The second identity
paragraphs: The line you had not seen before begins with inet, and the connection holding it is eth0 — the same connection whose factory identity you read in Mission 2. One connection, carrying both at once. Neither replaced the other.

The four numbers separated by dots, 192.168.1.10, are an IPv4 address. Unlike the factory identity, an IPv4 address is assigned: somebody chose it, it can be changed later, and it can be chosen deliberately so that machines meant to be grouped together are given addresses that look alike.

Hold the two apart, because they answer different questions. The MAC address you met in Mission 2 is built into the hardware, does not change, and identifies this particular piece of equipment wherever it goes. The IPv4 address is assigned to the machine where it currently sits, can be changed, and is about where this machine has been placed rather than what it is.

Say that in ordinary words before any more terminology arrives: one identity is which hardware this is, and the other is where this machine belongs. Both are true at the same time, both sit on the same connection, and both are things you can go and read rather than things you have to be told.

content.caption: A different machine on the same network, reporting the same way. This is displayed output again — nothing here offers to run anything, and the same few lines are shown out of the many a real machine prints. Notice before you start that this connection is not called eth0: connection names vary from machine to machine, and that is ordinary rather than a fault. Find this machine's IPv4 address, and say which connection holds it.

content.title: The same reading, on a machine that looks different
paragraphs: That was PC-B. Its connection is called enp0s3 rather than eth0, its factory identity ends c2 rather than b7, and its IPv4 address is 192.168.1.11 rather than 192.168.1.10.

Nothing about the reading itself changed. You looked for four numbers separated by dots, and you looked at which connection name they sat beneath. The name of the connection was not the thing you were looking for — it was only where you looked.

That distinction is worth keeping. Connection names are not standardised across machines, so a reader who has memorised the word eth0 is stuck the first time a machine disagrees with them. A reader who knows what shape of thing to look for is not.

This is also the habit the mission is really for. Being able to say what a machine actually holds, out of the machine's own report, is how you check a claim rather than trust it. You will do exactly this in every mission that follows.

content.title: What the address does not tell you yet
paragraphs: You can now read PC-A's IPv4 address and PC-B's. Here is a question you still cannot answer from them: which other addresses does PC-A treat as sitting on its own network, reachable directly in the way you watched in Mission 2 — and which does it not?

192.168.1.11 is PC-B, and you might reasonably guess that PC-A treats it as near. But guessing is not reading, and this course is about reading. What about 192.168.2.11? What about 10.0.0.5? Nothing you have looked at so far settles any of them.

So look again at what PC-A reported. The line read inet 192.168.1.10/24. You accounted for the four numbers separated by dots. You did not account for everything on that line — there is a part after the address that has said nothing to you yet, and it has been sitting there since the moment you first read it.

That is not an oversight in the output and it is not something you skipped over by accident. It is the piece of information the machine itself uses to draw a line between near and far, and reading it is the whole of the next mission.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Two identities on one connection: one built into the hardware, one assigned to the machine where it sits. You can find both, on any machine, out of the machine's own report — including on machines whose connections are not named the way you expected.

What you cannot do yet is say where PC-A's own network ends. PC-A holds an address. So far as you have read it, PC-A holds nothing that says which other addresses are close enough to reach the way Switch-1 delivered in Mission 2, and which are not.
It does hold that, and you have already looked straight at it without being able to use it. So carry one question into the next mission: what tells the machine where its local network ends?

missions.title: Mission 4 — The prefix, and the decision every host makes
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a machine's assigned address from real output (Mission 3), and compare two numbers.

This is the mission the rest of the course rests on.

An assigned address is written with a second number after it. That number says how much of the address names the group the machine belongs to, and how much names the machine itself. A larger number means more of the address is fixed and the group is smaller. You will compare two of them so the number stops being decoration and starts being a quantity.

With that, a machine can answer the only question that matters before it sends anything: is what I am trying to reach part of my own group, or not? Watch a machine answer it both ways. When the answer is yes, it delivers directly, using what you learned in Mission 2 — and you will see the small exchange it performs first to turn an assigned address into the factory identity it actually needs to address the traffic. When the answer is no, it does something you have not seen before: it hands the traffic to a different device entirely, one it was not trying to reach.

That hand-off will look wrong. Nothing was delivered to the destination, and yet nothing is broken. Deciding whether what you are watching is a fault or correct behaviour is the most useful question in this course, and this is the first place you get to ask it with enough information to answer.

You will not be told what that other device is called yet. You will see what it receives and why, and the name comes next.

By the end you will be able to take two machines' addresses and say whether one will deliver to the other directly, and say what it does instead when it will not.

content.title: Two destinations, one machine
paragraphs: PC-A holds 192.168.1.10. You read that off the machine yourself in Mission 3, and you read PC-B's 192.168.1.11 beside it.
Now PC-A is asked to reach two places, one after the other. First 192.168.1.11, which is PC-B. Then 192.168.2.20, which is a machine called PC-C that you have not met.
Both of those are addresses of exactly the same kind: four numbers separated by dots, read off a machine the same way. Nothing about how they are written tells you they are different sorts of thing.

PC-A does not treat them the same. Watch the first delivery, then watch the second, and the difference between them is what this mission is about. Do not try to work out the reason in advance — you have already seen the thing that explains it, and you have not been able to use it yet.

content.caption: PC-A reaching a destination inside its own group. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A network of five devices on one local network: PC-A, PC-B and a Printer, each with one interface, plus Switch-1 in the middle and Router-1 connected to Switch-1's fourth port. PC-A holds the address 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, PC-B holds 192.168.1.11 with 24 after it, and the Printer holds 192.168.1.12. Each interface also carries the hardware identity you met in Mission 2. The walkthrough follows PC-A being asked to reach 192.168.1.11. Before anything moves, PC-A asks itself one question: is that destination part of my own group? The 24 after its address is what answers it — it says the first three numbers of the address name the group rather than the machine, so PC-A's group is 192.168.1. The destination 192.168.1.11 is also 192.168.1, so it is in the same group, and PC-A concludes it can deliver directly. It cannot deliver yet, though. Mission 2 showed that Switch-1 delivers by hardware identity and never looks at an address like 192.168.1.11, and PC-A does not know the hardware identity of the machine holding that address. So PC-A asks for it: a question addressed to no one in particular, saying whoever holds 192.168.1.11 should reply with their hardware identity. That question arrives at Switch-1 on port 1, and Switch-1 sends a copy out of every other connection at the same moment — to PC-B, to the Printer and to Router-1. The Printer and Router-1 both compare the address against their own, find it is not theirs, and stay silent. PC-B recognises the address as its own and answers with its hardware identity, 00:1b:44:11:3a:c2. PC-A now holds both identities for the same machine, and delivery proceeds exactly as it did in Mission 2: Switch-1 receives it on port 1, finds PC-B recorded against port 2, and sends it out of port 2 alone. It reached PC-B directly, and Router-1 was never involved.

stages.narration: PC-A is asked to reach 192.168.1.11. Before anything moves, PC-A makes a decision — and it makes the same decision every time, for every destination.
stages.decision: The decision is one question: is this destination part of my own group, or not? Everything that happens next follows from the answer, so nothing leaves PC-A until the question is settled.

facts.label: Where it is asked to reach

stages.narration: PC-A settles it: 192.168.1.11 is part of its own group.
stages.decision: The part after the address is what settled it — the 24 you have been looking at since Mission 3 without being able to use it. It says how much of the address names the GROUP rather than the machine. Here it means the first three numbers are the group: 192.168.1. PC-A is 192.168.1.10 and the destination is 192.168.1.11, so both are 192.168.1, and they are in the same group.

stages.narration: PC-A is ready to deliver directly. It cannot yet.
stages.decision: Think back to Mission 2. Switch-1 never once looked at an address like 192.168.1.11 — it delivered by the factory identity written on each interface, and that is the only thing it records against a port. PC-A knows the destination's assigned address. It does not know that machine's factory identity, and without it there is nothing for Switch-1 to deliver to.

Ask the network, and let the machine that holds that address answer
Send to Router-1 instead and let it work out the rest

stages.narration: PC-A asks. The question is addressed to no one in particular — it says, in effect, whoever holds 192.168.1.11, tell me your factory identity. It reaches Switch-1 on port 1, and Switch-1 sends a copy out of every other connection at the same moment: to PC-B, to the Printer, and to Router-1.

stages.narration: PC-B recognises the address as its own and answers with its factory identity. The Printer and Router-1 both received the same question, compared it against their own addresses, and said nothing.
stages.decision: Nothing has gone wrong at the two machines that stayed silent. Being asked a question that turns out not to be yours is ordinary, and you watched the same thing happen to the Printer in Mission 2.

stages.narration: PC-A now has both identities for the same machine, and delivery proceeds exactly as it did in Mission 2: Switch-1 receives it on port 1, finds PC-B's factory identity recorded against port 2, and sends it out of port 2 alone.
stages.decision: Nothing new happened in this last step. That is the point — the second half of this delivery is Mission 2, unchanged. What Mission 4 added is everything that had to happen before Mission 2 could begin.

confirmation.narration: It reached PC-B, directly, without Router-1 being involved at all.
confirmation.summary: PC-A compared the destination against its own group and found it inside. That let it deliver directly — but delivering directly meant it first had to turn an assigned address into a factory identity, which it did by asking every machine on the network at once and letting the right one answer. After that, this was Mission 2 all over again.

content.title: What PC-A was reading
paragraphs: The number after the address is called the prefix length. It is the answer to the question Mission 3 left you holding: what tells the machine where its own group ends.

It works by splitting the address into two parts. The prefix length says how many of the leading digits name the network — the group the machine belongs to — and everything left over names the host, which is the individual machine inside that group. Those two parts are called the network portion and the host portion, and every address has both.

With 24, the split falls after the first three numbers. So in 192.168.1.10 the network portion is 192.168.1 and the host portion is 10. In 192.168.1.11 the network portion is 192.168.1 and the host portion is 11. The network portions match, so the two machines are on the same network — and that is the whole of the decision PC-A made before anything moved.

You are not being asked to calculate anything. You are being asked to read two addresses, see which part of each one names the network, and say whether those parts are the same. That is the question a machine asks before every single thing it sends, and you can now answer it yourself.

content.title: Turning one identity into the other
paragraphs: Deciding the destination was local was not enough to deliver to it, and the reason is Mission 2. Switch-1 delivers by hardware identity — the MAC address written on each interface — and it never looks at an address like 192.168.1.11 at all. PC-A had the wrong one of the two identities you have been carrying since Mission 3.
So PC-A asked for the other one. The request it sent is called ARP, and its job is exactly that: take an assigned address that belongs to this network, and find out which hardware identity holds it.

Notice what ARP is not. It is not a lookup in a list somebody configured, and it is not a service running somewhere. It is a question asked out loud on the local network, answered by whichever machine recognises the address as its own. Nobody arranged it in advance.

This is the moment the two identities finally connect. Mission 2 gave you the one a switch delivers by. Mission 3 gave you the one a person assigns. ARP is the step between them, and it only works for a destination on your own network — which is why PC-A had to settle the local question first.

content.title: Why everybody heard the question
paragraphs: Look again at how that question travelled. It arrived at Switch-1 on one port and left on every other one at the same moment — PC-B, the Printer and Router-1 all received it.

That is not the flooding you saw in Mission 2. Flooding happened because Switch-1 did not know where a destination was, and it stopped happening as soon as it learned. This is different: PC-A addressed the question to everybody on purpose, because it could not address it to anybody in particular. A message deliberately addressed to every machine on the local network is called a broadcast.

The distinction is worth keeping straight, because the two look identical on the picture and mean opposite things. Flooding is a switch not knowing yet. A broadcast is a sender deciding that everyone should hear it.

Two machines received the question, compared the address against their own, found it was not theirs, and said nothing. That is not a failure — it is every machine doing exactly what it should, and it is the same behaviour you watched the Printer perform in Mission 2.

content.title: The same question, a different destination
paragraphs: Now the second destination: 192.168.2.20.

Before you watch, work it out. PC-A holds 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, so its network portion is 192.168.1. Compare that against 192.168.2.20 and decide, for yourself, whether PC-A is going to treat this one the way it treated PC-B.
Then watch, and pay attention to what PC-A does NOT do, as much as to what it does.

content.caption: The same machine, asked to reach a destination outside its own group. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: The same local network as before — PC-A, PC-B, the Printer, Switch-1 and Router-1 — and beyond Router-1 a second machine, PC-C, holding the address 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it. PC-C is in a separate group of its own. The walkthrough follows PC-A being asked to reach 192.168.2.20. PC-A asks itself exactly the same question it asked before: is this destination part of my own group? It reads the same 24 after its own address, which says the first three numbers name the group, so its group is still 192.168.1. The destination is 192.168.2, and that differing number sits inside the part that names the group, so the answer this time is no. PC-A therefore does not ask the network for 192.168.2.20's hardware identity and does not attempt to deliver to it. Instead it hands what it is sending to Router-1, a device it was never trying to reach. Nothing was sent to PC-B or the Printer, and nothing arrived at 192.168.2.20 during the walkthrough. Nothing is broken. Why PC-A hands it to Router-1 in particular, and what Router-1 does with it afterwards, is not shown here.

confirmation.summary: The same machine, asking the same question, got the opposite answer and behaved completely differently. Inside its group it delivers directly. Outside its group it hands the traffic to Router-1 and stops being involved. Why Router-1, and what happens after that, is not something this mission has shown you.

content.title: Looks wrong, works as designed
paragraphs: PC-A was asked to reach 192.168.2.20 and sent what it was sending to Router-1, which is not 192.168.2.20 and never claimed to be. Nothing arrived at the destination in anything you watched.

In Mission 2 you were asked to form a habit: before deciding something is broken, ask whether it is the system working as designed. This is the second time that question has been worth asking, and this time you have enough to answer it.

It is working as designed. PC-A established that the destination is not on its own network. Everything PC-A can do by itself — ask on the local network, deliver by hardware identity — only works on its own network. So delivering this one was never PC-A's job, and handing it to Router-1 is PC-A correctly recognising the limit of what it can do.
That is a real and useful conclusion, and it is worth separating from the thing you still do not know. What PC-A did is settled. Why Router-1 is where it goes is not.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: You can now do the thing this mission was for: take two addresses, read which part of each names the network, and say whether one machine will deliver to the other directly — and say what it does instead when it will not.
The prefix length is no longer decoration. It is the number a machine consults before everything it sends.

One thing was left standing. PC-A sent to Router-1 without hesitating and without asking anyone, which means it was not working Router-1 out at the time — it already knew. Nothing you have looked at explains how it knew, or why Router-1 rather than any other device on the network.
So carry that into the next mission: how does PC-A know where to hand off, and why does it have to be that device in particular?

missions.title: Mission 5 — The default gateway
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: decide from two addresses whether a machine will deliver directly, and describe what it does instead when it will not (Mission 4).

In Mission 4 you watched a machine hand traffic to a device it was not trying to reach. That device has a name, and the machine did not guess at it — the address was configured in advance, and it is the machine's answer to "this is not for my group, so it is your problem now".

You will read that configuration from real output. There is one line in it that matters here, and you will learn to find that line and ignore the rest, which is a skill in itself.

Then you will work out why that address and not another. The device a machine hands traffic to has to be one the machine can reach directly, or the hand-off could never happen — which means it must be in the machine's own group. That single constraint explains almost every mistake people make with this setting, and you will meet one of those mistakes in Mission 8.

This is the smallest mission in the course, and deliberately so. It introduces one idea and one line of output. What that device actually does with the traffic once it has it is the next mission.

By the end you will be able to identify which address a machine will hand off to, and explain why that address has to be the one it is.

content.title: PC-A already knew
paragraphs: Go back to the last thing you watched in Mission 4. PC-A worked out that 192.168.2.20 was not in its own group, and then it handed what it was sending to Router-1.

Look at how it did that. It did not ask the network which device to use. It did not try several and keep the one that worked. There was no pause, no search and no question — PC-A turned to Router-1 immediately, the way you reach for something you already know the location of.
So PC-A was not working it out at the time. It already held the answer before the situation came up, which means somebody put the answer there in advance.

That is a fact about the machine, not about networks in general, and it means you can go and look. Read PC-A's own configuration and find the thing that told it where to send anything that was not local.

content.caption: PC-A's own configuration, as the machine reports it. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Two lines are shown, and only one of them can answer the question you are asking. Before you read on: work out which line tells PC-A where to send something that is NOT in its own group, and what the rest of each line is doing there.
content.output:
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto static metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.10

content.title: The line that answered it
paragraphs: It is the first one, and the part of it that matters is short: default via 192.168.1.1.

Read it plainly. By default — meaning when nothing more specific applies — send it via 192.168.1.1. That is a standing instruction, sitting on PC-A, waiting for exactly the situation Mission 4 produced.

Now look at the address itself, because you have seen it before. 192.168.1.1 is Router-1. You could read it on Router-1's connection in Mission 4, where it sat there without being explained. This is what it was for.

That standing instruction has a name: it is PC-A's default gateway. The setting holds one address, it is configured in advance rather than discovered, and it names the device a machine hands traffic to whenever the destination is not in its own group.

The second line is doing something else, and this is the part worth practising. It describes PC-A's own group — the one you learned to read in Mission 4 — and it is not what you were looking for. Neither is proto static, metric 100, proto kernel or scope link. Real output is mostly not the answer to the question you are asking, and finding the line that is has more to do with knowing what you are looking for than with understanding every word on the screen. You are not expected to know what all of those mean, and you do not need to.

content.title: Why it has to be one of your own
paragraphs: Here is a question you can now answer without being told, using only what Mission 4 gave you. Could PC-A's default gateway have been 192.168.2.1 instead?

Work it through. PC-A holds 192.168.1.10/24, so its group is 192.168.1. Handing something to the gateway is itself a delivery, and PC-A only has one way of delivering: the way you watched in Mission 4, directly, inside its own group. It has no other method.

So if the configured address were 192.168.2.1, PC-A would have to reach 192.168.2.1 in order to hand anything over — and 192.168.2.1 is not in its group, so reaching it would require handing it to the gateway first. The machine would need the gateway in order to reach the gateway.

That is why the constraint exists: a machine's default gateway has to be an address the machine can already reach directly, which means it has to be in the machine's own group. 192.168.1.1 satisfies that. 192.168.2.1 could not.
Notice that you did not need a new rule for this. You used the one you already had, and it settled the question on its own. That is worth more than the setting itself.

content.title: What happens after the hand-off
paragraphs: That is the whole of this mission, and it is deliberately small. PC-A holds one configured address for everything that is not local, that address is Router-1's, and it has to be Router-1's — or something else in PC-A's group — because a hand-off is a local delivery like any other.
You can now say where a machine sends remote traffic, find that setting in real output, and explain why it could not have been just any address.

What you still cannot say is what happens next. Router-1 now holds something addressed to a machine it is not, in a group it is not in. PC-A's involvement has ended and the traffic has not arrived anywhere.
So carry this into the next mission: what does Router-1 actually do with it?

missions.title: Mission 6 — Routers, and the journey end to end
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: identify the device a machine hands off to and explain why it must be reachable directly (Mission 5).

Everything so far has been one half of a trip. Now you follow a whole one.

A message leaves a machine in one group, crosses to a device that belongs to two groups at once, and comes out the other side into a group it was never part of. Watch what changes at that device and what does not. The destination does not change — it was decided before the message left and it survives the whole trip. What wraps around it is thrown away and rebuilt at every step, because each step is a different local delivery of the kind you learned in Mission 2.

That distinction — the part that survives the journey and the part that is rebuilt for each leg — is the single most useful idea in this course, and it only makes sense once you have watched it happen. You have now watched local delivery twice and a hand-off once, so it is time.

Then the reply comes back, the same way in reverse, and you watch that too. A trip that only goes one way is not communication.

At the end of this mission, and not before, you get two labels. The decisions about reaching someone in your own group have a common name. The decisions about reaching another group have a different one. These are names for behaviour you have already understood, not a framework to memorise. There are formal models that number these layers; you will meet them when you have a reason to, and this course does not give you one.

This mission introduces no new responsibility of its own. It puts five missions together into one continuous story, which is why nothing new is developed here and everything is used.

content.title: What Router-1 did with it
paragraphs: Mission 5 ended with something unfinished. PC-A had decided the destination was somewhere else, handed what it was sending to Router-1, and stopped being involved. Router-1 was holding something addressed to a machine it is not, in a group it is not in — and nothing had arrived anywhere.
That is the question you were asked to carry: what does Router-1 actually do with it?

You are about to watch the answer, and then watch the reply come back. Do not look for a new mechanism. Everything that happens in the next few minutes is something you have already seen, arranged in an order you have not.

One thing is worth deciding to pay attention to before you start. As it travels, some things about it stay the same the whole way and some things are replaced at every step. Watch for which is which. That distinction is what this mission is for.

content.caption: One exchange between PC-A and PC-C, out and back, across two networks. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A network of six devices across two networks. On the first: PC-A holding 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, PC-B holding 192.168.1.11, a Printer holding 192.168.1.12, and Switch-1 connecting all three plus Router-1. On the second: PC-C holding 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it, connected directly to Router-1. Router-1 is the only device in both: its local connection holds 192.168.1.1 and its second connection holds 192.168.2.1. Each machine also carries the hardware identity you have been reading since Mission 2. The walkthrough follows one exchange between PC-A and PC-C, out and back. PC-A has something for 192.168.2.20, decides as it did in Mission 4 that the destination is not in its group, and hands it to 192.168.1.1 as Mission 5 explained. The first leg is an ordinary local delivery: Switch-1 receives it on port 1 and sends it out of port 4 to Router-1, addressed to Router-1's hardware identity 00:1b:44:11:3a:01. Switch-1 has never heard of 192.168.2.20. It arrives at Router-1's local connection. Router-1 sees that the destination 192.168.2.20 is not itself and not on the network it arrived from, but is on the network its second connection belongs to, so it delivers it out of that connection — a second local delivery, on 192.168.2, addressed to PC-C's hardware identity 00:1b:44:11:3a:e4. The wrapper that carried it across the first network ended at Router-1 and a new one was built for the second. Where it was going never changed: 192.168.2.20 from beginning to end. PC-C then replies to 192.168.1.10, and performs the same reasoning in reverse: 192.168.1.10 is not in PC-C's group, so PC-C hands it to 192.168.2.1, Router-1's second connection. Router-1 receives it, finds 192.168.1.10 on its local connection's network, and delivers it there; Switch-1 carries it to port 1 and it arrives at PC-A. Four local deliveries on two networks. On every leg the delivery was addressed to a hardware identity on that leg's own network, and on no leg was that identity one of the two machines the exchange was actually between. Neither PC-A nor PC-C ever knew the other's hardware identity, and neither needed to. Nothing reached PC-B or the Printer at any point.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the machine that started this. It holds 192.168.1.10 and it decided, back in Mission 4, that 192.168.2.20 was not in its group. Everything it could do by itself is already done.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is on this network and has nothing to do with this trip. It is here because it was here in Missions 2, 3 and 4, and because a network does not empty itself when one machine starts talking.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer, still on port 3, still uninvolved. Watch that nothing in this whole journey ever reaches it.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 behaves exactly as it did in Mission 2 and has learned nothing new since. It delivers by hardware identity, on this network only, and it has no idea that anything on this network is trying to reach somewhere else.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 is the reason this trip is possible, and the reason is visible in its interfaces rather than in anything clever it does. It has one connection with an address in 192.168.1 and another with an address in 192.168.2. It is a member of both networks at once, which no other device here is.

nodes.label: PC-C
nodes.about: PC-C is the machine PC-A has been trying to reach since Mission 4. It holds 192.168.2.20, and like every machine you have met it holds one address for anything outside its own group — which here is Router-1's other connection.

traffic.label: what PC-A is sending to PC-C

stages.narration: PC-A has something for 192.168.2.20. You already know both halves of what happens next: the destination is not in its group, so PC-A will not deliver it directly, and PC-A holds one address for exactly this situation.
stages.decision: Nothing here is new. Mission 4 gave PC-A the decision and Mission 5 gave it the address. What has never been shown is what happens on the other side of that hand-off, and that starts one step from now.

facts.label: Where it is trying to reach

stages.narration: The first leg is an ordinary local delivery, exactly as in Mission 2. Switch-1 receives it on port 1 and sends it out of port 4, to Router-1, by hardware identity. PC-B and the Printer see nothing.
stages.decision: Look carefully at what Switch-1 is working from. It is delivering to 00:1b:44:11:3a:01, which is Router-1. It is not delivering to 192.168.2.20 and has never heard of it. Two different things are true at once, and keeping them apart is the whole of this mission.

stages.narration: It arrives at Router-1's local connection. Router-1 looks at where it is ultimately going — 192.168.2.20 — and that is not Router-1, and not on this network.
stages.decision: Router-1 is in a position no other device here is in. Its second connection holds 192.168.2.1, which is inside 192.168.2. The destination is inside 192.168.2. So the machine being looked for is reachable, directly, from Router-1's other side.

prediction.prompt: Router-1 is not 192.168.2.20, and 192.168.2.20 is not on the network this arrived from. Router-1's other connection holds 192.168.2.1. What does Router-1 do?
options: Sends it back to PC-A, because it is not the destination
Delivers it on its other connection, where that destination is local
Holds it until 192.168.2.20 asks for it

stages.narration: Router-1 delivers it out of its second connection, and it arrives at PC-C. That delivery was a local one, on 192.168.2, addressed to PC-C's hardware identity — the same kind of delivery Switch-1 performed on the first leg, on a different network.
stages.decision: The wrapper that carried it across the first network was finished the moment it reached Router-1, and a new one was built for the second network. What did not change is where it was going: 192.168.2.20 was decided by PC-A before anything moved, and it is still 192.168.2.20 now.

stages.narration: PC-C has it, and answers. Now watch PC-C do the same reasoning you watched PC-A do, from the other end.
stages.decision: PC-C holds 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it, so its group is 192.168.2. It is replying to 192.168.1.10, which is not in that group. So PC-C will not deliver directly either, and it hands to the one address it holds for everything outside its group.

prediction.prompt: PC-C holds 192.168.2.20/24 and must reply to 192.168.1.10. Apply the same rule PC-A applied. What does PC-C do?
options: Delivers directly to 192.168.1.10, because it is a reply
Hands it to 192.168.2.1, because 192.168.1.10 is outside its group
Sends it to every machine on its network to find the way back

facts.label: Where it is trying to reach

stages.narration: The reply travels the first leg of its own trip: a local delivery on 192.168.2, addressed to Router-1's second connection, and it arrives there.
stages.decision: Same shape as the outbound first leg, on the other network. A new wrapper again, built for this leg and finished at the end of it.

stages.narration: Router-1 looks at where the reply is ultimately going — 192.168.1.10 — and finds it inside 192.168.1, which is its local connection's network. So it delivers it there, and Switch-1 carries it to port 1.
stages.decision: Router-1 did the same thing in both directions. It received something not addressed to it, found which of its two connections that destination sits behind, and made an ordinary local delivery on that side.

stages.narration: It arrives at PC-A. The conversation PC-A started in Mission 4 has now happened in both directions.
stages.decision: Four local deliveries, on two networks, carrying one exchange between two machines that were never on the same network and never addressed each other's hardware. Neither PC-A nor PC-C ever knew the other's hardware identity, and neither needed to.

confirmation.narration: It reached PC-C, and the reply reached PC-A. Two machines on different networks, and neither ever knew the other's hardware identity.
confirmation.summary: One exchange, four local deliveries, two networks. On every single leg the delivery was made to a hardware identity on that leg's own network — and on no leg was that identity the machine the exchange was actually between. What stayed the same from beginning to end was where it was going. What was thrown away and rebuilt, four times, was the wrapper that got it across one network.

content.title: What survived, and what did not
paragraphs: Lay the four deliveries side by side. First leg: delivered to Router-1's hardware identity, on 192.168.1. Second leg: delivered to PC-C's hardware identity, on 192.168.2. Then the reply: to Router-1's other identity on 192.168.2, and finally to PC-A's on 192.168.1.

Four deliveries, four different hardware identities, two networks. Not one of those deliveries was addressed to the machine the exchange was actually between — except by accident at the very last step, where PC-A happened to be both.

Now lay the other thing beside it. From the moment PC-A decided to send, where it was going was 192.168.2.20. At Switch-1 it was still 192.168.2.20. At Router-1, still. On arrival, still. PC-A chose that before anything moved and nothing along the way altered it.

So two things were true at once for the whole journey, and they were doing different jobs. One of them said where this is ultimately for, and it survived every step. The other said who hands this to whom right now, on this network, and it was thrown away and rebuilt for each leg. Every hard part of networking gets easier once those two stop being the same thing in your head.

content.title: The two units
paragraphs: You already have a name for the one that gets rebuilt. In Mission 2 you watched something travel from one interface to another across a single network, addressed by hardware identity, and it was called a frame. That is exactly what each of those four legs was: a frame, built for one network, finished when it got to the other end of that network.

The thing inside it — the part that said 192.168.2.20 and kept saying it — is called a packet. A packet is addressed to where the exchange is ultimately going, and it does not care how many networks lie between here and there.

So the relationship is simple, and you watched it rather than being told it: one packet travelled from PC-A to PC-C, and it did so inside four different frames, because there were four separate local deliveries to make. The packet is the trip. A frame is one leg of it.

This is why Switch-1 could deliver something addressed to 192.168.2.20 without having any idea what 192.168.2.20 is. Switch-1 was never looking at the packet. It was delivering a frame, to a hardware identity, on its own network — which is all it has ever done.

content.title: What Router-1 was doing
paragraphs: Router-1 did the same thing twice, once in each direction, and it is worth saying plainly because it is less clever than it looks.

Something arrived that was not addressed to Router-1 and not going to a machine on the network it came from. Router-1 has two connections, each belonging to a different network. It looked at where the packet was ultimately going, worked out which of its connections that destination sits behind, and made an ordinary local delivery on that side — a new frame, on that network, to a hardware identity there.
Deciding which way to send a packet that is not for you, so that it gets closer to where it is going, is called routing. That is the whole of what Router-1 contributed to this journey.

Notice what routing needed. It needed a device belonging to more than one network at once, which is the only genuinely unusual thing about Router-1 and is visible in its two addresses. It did not need Router-1 to understand the conversation, know anything about PC-A or PC-C, or be told anything in advance beyond which networks its own connections are in.

content.title: Two kinds of decision
paragraphs: Every decision in this whole journey was one of exactly two kinds, and you can now sort them yourself.

Some were about getting something across one network, right now, to a hardware identity on that network: Switch-1 delivering to a port, PC-A addressing its frame to Router-1, Router-1 addressing its frame to PC-C. Those decisions never look beyond the network they happen on. Collectively they are called Layer 2.

The others were about where this is ultimately going, and whether the destination is in my group or somewhere else: PC-A deciding 192.168.2.20 was remote, Router-1 deciding which connection sits closer to it, PC-C deciding the same in reverse. Those decisions ignore hardware identities entirely and work in assigned addresses. Collectively they are called Layer 3.

Treat those two names as shorthand for behaviour you have already watched, because that is all they are here. There are formal models that number these layers and add more of them, and they are worth meeting when you have a reason to want them. You have not been given one, so this course does not hand you a diagram to memorise. You have something more useful: you can look at a decision and say which kind it is.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Five missions have come together into one trip. PC-A's local decision, the prefix that settled it, the hand-off address, the hardware identities the switch works from, and the topology you first read in Mission 1 — all of it was in play, and none of it was new.
You can now follow an exchange from one network to another and back, and say at every step which identity is being used, which one survives, and which one is about to be replaced.

There is something you cannot do yet, and it is a different kind of thing. Everything you just concluded, you concluded because you were shown it. You watched the frames being rebuilt. In front of a real network nobody shows you that, and the trip is not a picture — it either works or it does not, and you have to establish which from outside.
So carry this into the next mission: if nobody showed you, how would you find out whether any of that is actually happening?

missions.title: Mission 7 — Testing whether it actually works
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: follow a message from one group to another and back, and say what changes at each step (Mission 6).

So far you have been shown what happens. Now you find out for yourself.

There is a small test that asks a machine to answer, and reports whether it did. You will run it and read what comes back. Reading it is not the interesting part; deciding what to test is.

Here is the trap. A test that succeeds proves something specific, and it is almost never the thing people assume it proves. If a machine can reach the device it hands off to, that proves the first step works and says nothing about the rest of the trip. If it cannot reach that device, then nothing beyond it can possibly work, and testing anything further is wasted effort. Choosing what to test, in what order, so that each result actually narrows things down, is a different skill from running the test.

You will practise the difference between a result that confirms what you believe and a result that is merely consistent with it. Those feel identical in the moment and are not the same, and telling them apart is what separates someone who is checking from someone who is guessing.

By the end you will be able to choose which address to test in order to establish a specific claim, and say what a successful result does and does not prove.

content.title: Nobody draws it for you
paragraphs: In Mission 6 you followed one exchange from PC-A to PC-C and back, and you could say at every step which identity was being used and which one survived. You knew all of that for one reason: the course showed you.
Take the drawing away. PC-A is in front of you, the same network is behind it, and nothing is animated. You believe the trip works. Somebody asks you how you know.
You cannot follow it. You cannot see the frames being rebuilt. Everything you understood was visible only because it was drawn for you, and none of it is visible now.

What you can do is ask. If a machine will answer you, that answer is something you observed rather than something you were told — and an answer you can get from outside is worth more than a diagram you have to trust. So the question this mission is really about is not how to ask. It is what an answer entitles you to conclude.

This is displayed output for you to read; nothing here offers to run anything, and no live network is involved. Before you read on, decide for yourself: this succeeded, so what does it prove?

content.title: What that actually proves
paragraphs: The tool is called ping. It asks one address to answer, and reports whether it did. It works by sending a small message whose only purpose is to be replied to — a kind of message called ICMP, which exists for asking and answering questions about the network rather than for carrying anything of your own. That is as much as you need about ICMP to stop ping being magic.
Now the part that matters. Three asks, three replies, nothing lost. Something answered from 192.168.1.1. Work out carefully what had to be true for that to happen.

PC-A had to build the ask and put it onto its own network. Switch-1 had to deliver it by hardware identity, which means PC-A had to know that identity, which means the exchange from Mission 4 had already happened. Router-1 had to receive it and answer, and the answer had to come back the same way. So the first leg of the trip — PC-A to Router-1 and back — works. That is a real conclusion and it is worth having.

Here is what it does not give you. It says nothing about whether PC-C is reachable, nothing about whether Router-1 can deliver onto the other network, nothing about whether the far side is even switched on. It certainly does not establish that the network works. Every one of those is a claim about something the ask never went near, and a result cannot be evidence about a path it did not take.

This is displayed output for you to read; nothing here offers to run anything, and no live network is involved. Before you read on: this also succeeded, so what does it let you conclude that the previous result did not?
