content.title: Confirms, or merely consistent with
paragraphs: Something answered from 192.168.2.20, and that is a much larger result than the first one. For an answer to come back from there, the whole trip you watched in Mission 6 had to happen — out through Router-1 onto the other network, and back again. A reply cannot arrive unless the return path also worked. One successful answer from the far side establishes the round trip, for that address, at that moment.

Put the two results side by side, because the difference between them is the whole point of this mission. Both succeeded. Both look equally reassuring. They entitle you to completely different conclusions.

Suppose you believe the network is fine and you test 192.168.1.1. It answers. Does that confirm your belief? No — it is merely consistent with it. A working network would produce that result, and so would a network where Router-1's far side is unplugged, and so would a network where PC-C has been switched off for a week. A result that every one of those situations would produce cannot tell you which one you are in.

Now test 192.168.2.20 instead. It answers. That result is not consistent with the far side being unplugged, or with PC-C being off, because neither of those could have produced a reply. It rules out the alternatives rather than merely fitting alongside them, and that is what makes it evidence for the claim rather than decoration next to it.

This is the habit worth taking away, and it costs nothing to apply: after any result, ask what else would have produced exactly the same thing. If the answer is "quite a lot", you have not learned as much as it feels like you have.

content.title: Choosing what to ask first
paragraphs: You now have two tests that establish different things, so you get to choose which to run — and the order is not arbitrary.
Consider a case you have not seen. Suppose PC-A could not reach 192.168.1.1 at all. Nothing answered. Before reading on, decide: would it be worth testing 192.168.2.20 next?

It would not, and the topology tells you why without any need to guess. Everything PC-A sends to the other network goes to Router-1 first — that is what Mission 5 established, and Mission 6 showed every leg of it. If PC-A cannot reach the one device it hands everything off to, then nothing beyond that device can possibly be reachable either. A test of 192.168.2.20 would fail, and it would fail for a reason you already knew, which means it would tell you nothing you did not already have.

That is what makes a good first test. Not the one that answers the question you care about most, but the one whose result changes what you do next. A test that could only ever tell you something you already knew is not a diagnostic step, however easy it is to run.

So the ordering follows the path. Ask about the nearest thing that has to work, and only move outward once you know it does. Nothing is wrong here, and you are not being asked to find anything. You are learning to choose, before there is any pressure to choose well.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Everything you tested in this mission worked. Both asks were answered, and the only thing you had to be careful about was not claiming more than the answers supported.

What you can now do is pick an address to ask about in order to establish one specific claim, and say afterwards what that result does and does not settle. That is a different skill from knowing how a network works, and it is the one that survives contact with a real one.
It has been easy so far because nothing has been wrong. Every result has agreed with what you expected, which means you have never had to act on one.
That changes next. Something is going to fail, and the reasoning you have just practised is what turns a failure from a frustration into a starting point.

missions.title: Mission 8 — When it does not work
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: choose a test that establishes a specific claim, and say what its result proves (Mission 7).

Something is wrong, and this time it really is wrong.

A message leaves and does not arrive. You will watch where it stops. You are shown the stopping point in this mission — you are not yet being asked to find a failure nobody has located for you, which is a harder skill and belongs to a later course. What you are asked to do here is reason about what a visible stopping point tells you.

Work backwards from it. The last thing that behaved correctly tells you what is still intact. The first thing that did not tells you where to look. Everything you have built across seven missions is what makes that reasoning possible: you know what should have happened at each step, so you can tell which step did not do it.

The cause is a single wrong setting, of a kind you were warned about in Mission 5. Correct it, and then — this is the part that matters — watch the message go the whole way and the reply come back. A repair you did not confirm is not a repair; it is a hope. The confirmation is not a formality at the end of the mission, it is the point of it.

By the end you will have taken a bounded failure from symptom to evidence to correction to proof, which is the shape of every piece of troubleshooting you will ever do.

This mission develops no new responsibility. It is where everything the course built gets used at once, which is the only honest test of whether it was built properly.

competencies.title: Network topology literacy
competencies.description: Identify the hosts, switches and routers in a network topology, name the interfaces and ports that connect them, and state which device is responsible for each part of a path between two machines.

competencies.title: Local network delivery
competencies.description: Explain how a switch delivers traffic to one host within a single network, how it learns where hosts are, what it does with a destination it has not learned, and why traffic for another network is handed elsewhere.

competencies.title: IPv4 address identification
competencies.description: Identify the IPv4 address assigned to a host's interface, read it from device or operating-system output, and distinguish an assigned address from the interface's built-in hardware identity.

competencies.title: IPv4 addressing
competencies.description: Assign and interpret an IPv4 address and prefix length, and determine which addresses a host can reach without assistance from a router.

competencies.title: Subnet boundaries
competencies.description: Determine from an address and prefix length whether two hosts share a subnet, and recognise the boundary at which forwarding becomes a router's responsibility.

competencies.title: Default gateway relationships
competencies.description: Identify the correct default gateway for a host and explain why off-subnet traffic depends on it.

competencies.title: Connectivity verification
competencies.description: Choose verification steps that establish what actually works, and distinguish a test that confirms a hypothesis from one merely consistent with it.
